paragraphs: F. Scott Fitzgerald was born in 1896 in St. Paul, Minnesota, into a family of modest means that nevertheless moved in the shadow of great wealth. He was a young man of brilliant talent and restless ambition who fell in love, in the America of the 1920s, with two things at once: money and the people who had it. He married Zelda Sayre, a celebrated Southern belle, and together they became the emblematic couple of the Jazz Age, living hard in New York and Paris, spending everything they earned. Fitzgerald died in 1940, at only forty-four, believing himself a failure. The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, sold poorly in his lifetime. Only after his death did the world recognize it as one of the greatest novels ever written in English.

The novel is the definitive portrait of the Jazz Age, the roaring 1920s decade after the First World War, when America grew suddenly, dizzyingly rich. Prohibition had made drinking illegal and bootlegging glamorous; the stock market climbed; jazz poured out of every speakeasy; and a whole generation, having survived the trenches, decided to live as if tomorrow did not exist. Fitzgerald saw the glitter and the rot at the same time. The Great Gatsby is at once a love story, a murder story, and an autopsy of the American Dream itself: the belief that anyone can become anyone, that wealth can buy happiness, that the past can be repeated. It cannot, and the novel knows it.

The story is told by Nick Carraway, a young Midwesterner who moves east in the summer of 1922 and finds himself living next door to the mysterious Jay Gatsby, the richest and loneliest man on Long Island. Nick is our eyes: decent, observant, a little naive, and by the end quietly broken by everything he has witnessed. What follows is an essential selection of the novel's most important passages and scenes, retold faithfully, with its most famous lines preserved in Fitzgerald's own words.

Fitzgerald wrote the novel out of his own life. At twenty-four, his first novel, This Side of Paradise, had made him famous overnight, and he married Zelda Sayre, the golden girl he had been chasing. For a decade they lived the Jazz Age from the inside: New York, the Riviera, Paris, endless parties, endless spending. Fitzgerald knew the rich intimately and never quite belonged to them, and that double vision, enchanted and critical at once, is the engine of the novel. He wrote Gatsby in France in 1924, in a villa on the Riviera, with money running out and his marriage fraying, pouring into it everything he understood about longing.

When it appeared in 1925, the book was admired but not loved. It sold modestly, the reviews were mixed, and Fitzgerald died fifteen years later believing it a failure. The revival came after the Second World War, when the novel was reissued and a new generation recognized it as the great American novel of the century. Today it is read in schools around the world, quoted in politics and pop culture, and endlessly adapted. It endures because its subject never ages: the distance between what we dream and what we get, and the beautiful, ruinous human habit of confusing money with happiness.
chapters.title: Introduction: Fitzgerald and the Jazz Age

paragraphs: In the summer of 1922, Nick Carraway came east to New York to learn the bond business. He was twenty-nine, a Yale graduate from a solid Midwestern family, and he rented a small weather-beaten bungalow in West Egg, Long Island, for eighty dollars a month. It was an odd little house squeezed between enormous mansions, and it stood directly beside the colossal estate of a man Nick had never met: Jay Gatsby.

Long Island's north shore, in those days, was divided by money into two Eggs. West Egg, where Nick lived, was the less fashionable side, home to the newly rich, people who had made their fortunes quickly and spent them loudly. East Egg, across the bay, was older money, whiter, more established, more certain of itself. On the East Egg shore stood the colonial mansion of Tom and Daisy Buchanan. Daisy was Nick's cousin, once removed, and he had not seen her in years. He decided to pay a call.

The Buchanans' house was a cheerful red-and-white Georgian colonial mansion overlooking the bay, with a lawn that ran down to the water and French windows glowing in the evening. Inside, everything moved with a kind of restless brightness. Tom Buchanan was enormous, a former Yale football star with a cruel mouth and a body that seemed to carry its own violence. Daisy was lovely in a way that made the room seem to lean toward her: her voice was low and thrilling, a voice that promised excitement, and she had the habit of laughing as if there were no such thing as sadness in the world.

They had been married for three years and had a little daughter, Pammy, who was mostly in the care of a nurse. But the marriage was already hollow. Over dinner, while Daisy talked brightly of everything and nothing, Tom took a telephone call from another room, and Jordan Baker, the young woman visiting the Buchanans, leaned toward Nick and murmured the open secret of the house: Tom had a woman in New York. Jordan was a professional golfer, slender and cool, with a bored, charming detachment, and she delivered the information the way one mentions the weather.

Nick soon learned the details. The woman was Myrtle Wilson, the wife of a garage owner in the valley of ashes, a desolate stretch of industrial wasteland between West Egg and New York City, where the ashes of the city grew into gray hills and men moved dimly among them. Tom kept an apartment for Myrtle in Manhattan, on 158th Street, where they drank and quarreled with a circle of hangers-on. Nick was dragged there one afternoon and watched the whole sordid performance: Myrtle, a coarse, vital woman in her thirties, putting on airs in a new dress; Tom, swaggering and brutal; the whiskey flowing. When Myrtle, drunk, began chanting Daisy's name with mocking familiarity, Tom's hand shot out and broke her nose with one short, decisive blow. Nobody was particularly shocked. That was Tom: money had given him a sense of ownership over the world, and violence was simply one of the ways he held it. Nick left the apartment that night sick and shaken, having glimpsed the ugliness underneath the glitter of this new rich world.

Between West Egg and New York lay the valley of ashes, a fantastic farm where ashes grew like wheat into ridges and hills and grotesque gardens. It was the dumping ground of the city, gray and desolate, where ash-gray men moved dimly among the cinders with spades and vacant eyes. Above it all, on a fading billboard, the enormous eyes of an oculist named T. J. Eckleburg stared out over the wasteland, blue and gigantic, their retinas one yard high. The eyes did not blink. They watched the ash, the men, the cars passing on the road to the city, like the eyes of some abandoned god. In the middle of this desolation stood Wilson's garage, a small block of yellow brick, where George Wilson repaired cars and his wife Myrtle dreamed of escape.

At dinner in the Buchanan house, the conversation kept sliding toward money and power. Tom held forth about a book he had been reading, a pseudo-scientific tract arguing that the white race was being submerged by other races and must assert its dominance or perish. He delivered these ideas with the heavy confidence of a man who believed civilization depended on men like him. Daisy mocked him lightly, calling him a brute and changing the subject, but there was an edge to her laughter. When Tom left the room to take the telephone call from New York, Daisy leaned toward Nick and spoke of her daughter Pammy with a sudden, startling bitterness. She said she had been glad when she learned the baby was a girl, and she hoped the girl would grow up to be a beautiful little fool, because that was the best thing a girl could be in this world. Nick was shocked by the cynicism in her lovely voice. It was the first crack in Daisy's brightness, the first hint that she understood exactly how hollow her gilded life was.

The apartment party on 158th Street was Nick's full introduction to Tom's other life. The flat was a small, crowded living room full of borrowed furniture and loud people: Mr. McKee, a pale feminine photographer, and his shrill wife; Myrtle's sister Catherine, worldly and hard; and Myrtle herself, transformed by a new cream-colored chiffon dress into a parody of the society women she envied. The whiskey flowed, the gossip turned cruel, and Myrtle held court, complaining about her husband, whom she described as too dumb to know he was alive, and boasting about Tom's wealth as if it were her own. Tom moved through it all with the complacency of a man who owned the room and everyone in it.

When Myrtle, drunk and reckless, began taunting Tom by chanting Daisy's name, daring him to hit her, the evening turned ugly in an instant. Tom's open hand shot out and broke her nose, and blood poured over her dress while the McKees fled and Catherine pretended nothing had happened. Nobody called a doctor with any urgency; nobody confronted Tom. Nick sat there sickened, realizing that this was what unlimited money did to a man like Tom: it removed every consequence, every restraint. He slipped out into the late night, rode down in the elevator with Mr. McKee, and walked home through the dark streets, his head full of the evening's sordidness. He had come east seeking sophistication and success. What he had found, in his first weeks, was brutality dressed in evening clothes.
chapters.title: West Egg and the Buchanans

paragraphs: Every Friday, five crates of oranges and lemons arrived at Gatsby's mansion, and every Saturday night the place blazed with light and music. Gatsby's parties were the most extravagant on Long Island: an orchestra played under the stars, the gardens filled with hundreds of guests, the bars never closed, and the champagne flowed like water. People came who had never been invited and would never be invited again. They danced on the lawns, they swam in the pool, they gossiped about their host, a man almost no one had actually met. Was he a German spy? A murderer? Had he killed a man once? The rumors multiplied because the truth was unknown.

Nick received something almost no one else did: a formal invitation, hand-delivered by Gatsby's chauffeur. On a warm Saturday night he walked across his own lawn into the carnival next door. The party was a confusion of laughter, music, and drifting groups of strangers. Nick knew no one and felt absurdly alone until he fell into conversation with a pleasant man in his early thirties, in a white flannel suit, who seemed as much a guest as Nick was. They talked easily about the war, about the Middle West. Only when the man smiled, a rare, reassuring smile that seemed to understand exactly what Nick was feeling, did Nick realize whom he was talking to. It was Gatsby himself.

Gatsby apologized for not having called on Nick sooner and insisted Nick come over for a swim, for anything, anytime. He had a habit of calling everyone old sport, a phrase that sounded oddly rehearsed, as if he had picked it up from somewhere and was still trying it on. There was something gorgeous about him, Nick thought, a heightened sensitivity to the promises of life, as if he were related to one of those intricate machines that register earthquakes ten thousand miles away. But there was also something guarded, something performed. When Nick mentioned that he lived next door, Gatsby seemed oddly pleased, almost relieved, and asked Nick about his plans for the summer with an intensity that went beyond politeness.

Later that night, driving home with Jordan Baker, Nick learned that Gatsby's interest in him was not accidental. Jordan revealed that Gatsby had asked her, with elaborate casualness, whether Nick might invite Daisy Buchanan to tea one afternoon, alone, without telling her that Gatsby would be there. Daisy and Gatsby had known each other five years before, in Louisville, before the war. Gatsby had never stopped thinking about her. The parties, the mansion, the fortune itself, all of it had been built for one purpose: to bring Daisy Buchanan back across the bay. Nick was being asked to arrange the reunion. Gatsby's whole glittering empire was a stage set, and Daisy was the only audience that mattered.

The preparations alone were a spectacle. Every Friday, the grounds filled with caterers and florists; buffet tables were set up in the gardens under acres of canvas; the bars were stocked with the rarest liquors; and by seven o'clock on Saturday the orchestra had arrived, a whole pit full of oboes and trombones and saxophones and viols and cornets and piccolos, drums and banjos, playing yellow cocktail music while the guests began to stream in. Cars from all over Long Island and New York parked five deep in the drive. The sea-change of faces and voices and color under the constantly changing light made the party feel less like an entertainment than like a force of nature, something Gatsby had summoned and could barely control.

The guests came from everywhere and knew nothing about their host. A guest list Nick later saw read like a directory of the Jazz Age demimonde: theater people, brokers, bootleggers, a man who fixed the World Series, divorcées, film directors, cousins and hangers-on. They drank his liquor and ate his food and repaid him with gossip. Gatsby, they said, was the nephew of Kaiser Wilhelm, or a German spy, or had killed a man, or had been a bootlegger himself. One woman claimed he was an Oxford man; another swore he had once been seen with a gangster in Chicago. The rumors grew wilder precisely because Gatsby himself drifted through his own parties like a guest, smiling, shaking hands, introducing himself to people who had been coming for weeks without ever meeting him.

In the Gothic library, Nick stumbled on the strangest detail of all. A stout, owl-eyed man in spectacles sat poring drunkenly over the shelves and called Nick over in amazement: the books were real. Real books, with pages and everything, not cardboard stage props. The owl-eyed man took it as a marvelous joke on reality, proof that Gatsby was a real Belasco, a theatrical producer of life itself. But Nick saw it differently. The real books meant Gatsby's performance went all the way down; even the props were genuine. It was one of the novel's quietest revelations: Gatsby believed in his own invention so completely that he had furnished it with real pages.

Nick's second party came with Daisy and Tom in tow, and it changed everything. Daisy, seeing Gatsby's world for the first time, was dazzled but also faintly repelled by its raw vigor. She danced with Gatsby, and for a moment Nick saw them as the lovers they had been in Louisville. But Tom, prowling the edges of the party with his polo-player's arrogance, was already suspicious. He cornered Nick and demanded to know who Gatsby really was, and when Nick mentioned Oxford, Tom scoffed openly. Afterward, driving home, Daisy said the party had been too much, too crowded, too wild. Gatsby, overhearing, was crushed. Nick tried to reassure him, but he could see the truth: Daisy belonged to a world that would never fully accept Gatsby's, no matter how beautiful the shirts. The parties stopped soon after. Gatsby fired his servants and closed the carnival down, because the only guest he had ever wanted had finally come, and one guest was enough.
chapters.title: Gatsby's Parties

paragraphs: One evening, before any of this was clear to him, Nick came home late from New York and saw something that stayed with him. Gatsby's mansion blazed with light as always, but Gatsby himself was standing alone on his lawn in the dark, his arms stretched out toward the water in a curious, trembling gesture. Nick looked where he was looking and could make out nothing except a single green light, minute and far away, at the end of a dock across the bay. It was the dock of the Buchanan house in East Egg. Daisy was there, on the other side of the water, and Gatsby stood in the dark reaching toward her light.

Nick did not know yet what the light meant, but the image lodged in his mind: the richest man on Long Island, alone in the darkness, stretching out his arms toward something he could see but never touch. It was the perfect picture of longing, and Nick understood, without yet understanding why, that he had witnessed something private and enormous. He wanted to call out to Gatsby, to say something, but he did not. He went inside his own small house and left Gatsby there with his green light.

Only much later did Nick grasp the full meaning of what he had seen. The green light was Daisy, or rather what Daisy represented: youth, beauty, wealth, the whole shimmering promise of a life Gatsby had been denied as a poor boy and had spent five years chasing. It stood at the end of Daisy's dock, green like the green of spring, like go-lights and growing things, like the future itself. Gatsby did not want Daisy the person so much as he wanted the dream she embodied, the dream of becoming someone else entirely. The light was always across the water. That was the point. It had to stay just out of reach, or the dream would die.

The light itself was an ordinary thing: a small green lamp at the end of a dock, the kind of light that marks a channel for boats. Daisy had probably never given it a thought. But to Gatsby it had become the most important object in the world, the visible form of everything he wanted. Green is the color of go-lights and growing things, of spring and money and the future, and Fitzgerald chose it deliberately. The light was always across the water, always just beyond reach, and that distance was essential. A dream that can be touched stops being a dream. Gatsby needed the light to stay far away, because the far-away-ness was what made it holy.

Nick would later understand that the green light was the perfect symbol of the American Dream itself: the belief that happiness lies just ahead, across the water, in the next fortune, the next love, the next reinvention. America had been founded on that belief, on the idea that the future would always be larger and brighter than the past. Gatsby was that belief in human form, a man who had taken the national promise absolutely literally. His tragedy was not that he dreamed too much but that he dreamed of the wrong thing: he believed a person could be a destination, that Daisy could be the green light, when in fact the light was always going to recede.

There is a reason the image of Gatsby with his arms outstretched has become one of the most famous in all of literature. It captures something every reader recognizes: the posture of longing itself. We have all stood in the dark reaching toward something we cannot have, certain that it is real, certain that it is close, unable to stop reaching. Fitzgerald gives us the gesture without explaining it, and lets it do its work. Long after the parties and the shirts and the yellow car are forgotten by a first-time reader, the man on the lawn with his arms out toward the green light remains, trembling in the dark, reaching across the water toward everything he cannot touch.
chapters.title: The Green Light

paragraphs: Jay Gatsby was born James Gatz, a poor farm boy from North Dakota, the son of shiftless and unsuccessful farm people. From the beginning he was different from his parents. As a boy he dreamed constantly of becoming someone else, someone rich and powerful and admired. When he was seventeen, he found a battered copy of a cowboy novel and wrote on its last page a schedule for his own self-improvement: rising at six, exercising, studying electricity and mechanics, practicing elocution and poise, reading improving books. It was the plan of a boy who believed that a man could invent himself from nothing, by will alone.

His chance came on the shore of Lake Superior. He was working as a clam digger and salmon fisher when he saw a yacht anchored offshore in a storm: the yacht of Dan Cody, a millionaire who had made a fortune in copper and lived a wild, drunken life at sea. Young Gatz rowed out through the rough water to warn Cody, and Cody, impressed by the boy's nerve, took him aboard. For five years Gatz sailed with Cody as his steward, his mate, his companion, learning the ways of wealth at close range: how the rich talked, dressed, drank, and wasted. When Cody died, Gatz expected to inherit twenty-five thousand dollars, but Cody's mistress cheated him out of it through the lawyers, and he got nothing. What he kept was more valuable to him than money: the education, and the proof that a farm boy could live among millionaires. It was on Cody's yacht that James Gatz became Jay Gatsby, inventing the person he intended to be.

Then came the war. Gatsby was sent to officer training at Camp Taylor in Louisville, Kentucky, and there, in the autumn of 1917, he met Daisy Fay, the most beautiful and most desired girl in Louisville, a girl whose white dresses and golden voice seemed to embody everything lovely and expensive in the world. Daisy lived in the glow of wealth without quite possessing it herself, and Gatsby, a young lieutenant with a borrowed uniform and a fabricated past, fell in love with her with the full force of his invented self. For a month they were together, and in that month he took her, and she took him, and something in him was changed forever. When he was shipped to France, Daisy promised to wait, but she did not. In 1919 she married Tom Buchanan of Chicago, a brutal, enormously rich polo player, and Gatsby, returning from the war decorated and empty-handed, learned of the marriage from a newspaper clipping he carried for years.

Gatsby refused to accept it. He went to Oxford for a few months on a veterans' program, then came home and devoted himself to a single purpose: becoming rich enough that Daisy would have to notice him. He fell in with Meyer Wolfsheim, a gambler and bootlegger, and made his fortune in the shadow economy of Prohibition: bonds, liquor, drugstores that were fronts, the whole underworld apparatus that turned the 1920s into a carnival of easy money. He bought the mansion in West Egg precisely because it faced Daisy's house across the bay. He threw his extravagant parties hoping that one night Daisy would wander in by chance. For five years he lived in the service of a dream, waiting, accumulating, believing that if he only shone brightly enough, the past could be repeated and Daisy would come back to him. It was the most romantic and the most doomed project in American literature: a man trying to buy his way back in time.

The five years with Dan Cody were Gatsby's university. Cody was fifty, a product of the Nevada silver fields and the Yukon, a millionaire many times over who had grown lonely and reckless with his fortune. He took the boy from North Dakota everywhere: up and down the coast, to the West Indies, to South America, drinking and spending and living the wild life of the very rich at sea. Gatsby learned it all: the clothes, the manners, the casual waste, the way money made everything easy and nothing satisfying. When Cody died, his mistress Ella Kaye played the victim so skillfully that she walked away with the entire fortune, leaving Gatsby with nothing but his education. It was his first lesson in what money really does to people, though he refused to learn it.

The war gave Gatsby his decorations and took his girl. He fought in the Argonne with valor, was promoted to major, and received medals from two countries. He carried himself like a gentleman officer because he had spent five years studying how gentlemen behaved. But while he was in France, Daisy did what girls of her class did: she married well. Tom Buchanan, rich beyond anything Gatsby could then imagine, offered her the life she had been raised to expect, and Daisy, who loved comfort more than she loved waiting, accepted. Gatsby's furlough came too late. He arrived in Louisville to find Daisy gone, and he carried the newspaper clipping of her wedding for years, like a wound he refused to let heal.

After the Armistice, Gatsby spent five months at Oxford on a veterans' program, a detail Tom would later sneer at but which was perfectly true. Then he came home to nothing: no family money, no prospects, no Daisy. It was then that he met Meyer Wolfsheim, the gambler who had fixed the 1919 World Series, a man who wore cufflinks made of human molars and spoke of the underworld as a business like any other. Wolfsheim saw in Gatsby a young man of nerve and ambition, and he put him to work. The money came from everywhere Prohibition made profitable: bootlegged liquor, bonds of dubious origin, drugstores that sold grain alcohol over the counter. Within three years, James Gatz of North Dakota had become Jay Gatsby of West Egg, rich enough to buy the mansion across the bay from Daisy. He told himself the money was only a means. In a way, it was the purest motive in the book. In every other way, it was the trap that would kill him.

Gatsby's reinvention was total. He changed his name, invented an Oxford past, bought the right clothes, learned the phrase old sport from somewhere and wore it like a borrowed suit. He even changed his history so completely that he half-believed it himself. But the reinvention had one flaw, and it was fatal: it was all built for an audience of one. The mansion, the parties, the cars, the pink suits, the fortune itself, none of it meant anything except as a signal to Daisy across the water. Gatsby had become the richest man on Long Island in order to become, once again, the young officer Daisy had loved in Louisville. He was trying to purchase the past with the future's money, and Fitzgerald never lets us forget the impossibility of the exchange.
chapters.title: James Gatz

paragraphs: Nick agreed to arrange the meeting, though the request embarrassed him. On the appointed afternoon it rained, and Gatsby arrived at Nick's cottage an hour early, so nervous he could barely stand still. He paced the small living room, stared out the window at the wet lawn, and sent a gardener over to cut Nick's grass. When Daisy finally arrived, Gatsby had vanished; Nick found him outside in the rain, pale and damp, looking like a man about to faint. He led Gatsby back inside, and there was Daisy, and for a moment the two of them stood in Nick's living room in a terrible, wonderful awkwardness, while Gatsby, leaning against the mantelpiece, nearly knocked the clock off in his agitation.

Then Nick, with sudden tact, went outside for half an hour and walked around in the rain. When he returned, everything had changed. The sun was out, Gatsby was radiant, Daisy was glowing, and the two of them were talking as if the five lost years had never happened. Gatsby insisted on showing Daisy his mansion, and the three of them walked through the vast empty rooms: the music room, the bedrooms with their period furniture, the bathrooms with sunken tubs, while Gatsby pointed out everything with the pride of a boy showing off a treehouse. Daisy admired it all, and something in her voice suggested she was overwhelmed not just by the house but by the scale of what Gatsby had done for her.

Then came the shirts. In Gatsby's dressing room, his servant brought out stack upon stack of shirts, piled like bricks in every color and pattern: stripes and plaids, coral and apple-green and lavender, monograms in Indian blue. Gatsby began throwing them onto the table in a soft, rich heap, and as the pile grew higher, Daisy bent her head into the shirts and began to cry stormily. The beauty of the shirts, the sheer gorgeous waste of them, broke something open in her. She had never seen such beautiful shirts, and the tears came because she understood at last what Gatsby's love looked like when it was translated into things. It is the saddest and most tender moment in the novel: Daisy weeping not for Gatsby the man but for the beautiful, impossible world he had built out of longing for her.

From that afternoon on, the affair was rekindled. Daisy began coming to Gatsby's parties, and Gatsby, drunk on happiness, told Nick the whole story of Louisville and the war and the five years of waiting. He spoke with the absolute certainty of a man describing a fact: Daisy loved him, had always loved him, and Tom was nothing, an accident, an interruption. Gatsby believed, truly believed, that he could erase the years of Daisy's marriage as if they had never happened, that Daisy would tell Tom she had never loved him and they would go back to Louisville and be married from her house, just as if it were five years ago. It was a magnificent, childlike faith, and Nick, listening, felt both moved and afraid, because he could see what Gatsby could not: that you cannot repeat the past, however beautiful the shirts.

The reunion had its comic moments too. Before Daisy arrived, Gatsby had sent over a greenhouse full of flowers, transforming Nick's shabby cottage into a bower, and he kept rearranging the details with frantic precision. When the rain finally stopped and the sun came out, Gatsby looked at Nick's humble rooms with sudden embarrassment, as if seeing them for the first time through Daisy's eyes. But Daisy did not care about the cottage. She cared only that Gatsby was there, real and alive, after five years of being a memory. They sat on Nick's porch and talked, and the years fell away, and for an hour the impossible seemed possible.

At the mansion, Gatsby showed them everything, and the tour became a kind of courtship. He opened the music room, the salon, the bedrooms; he showed Daisy the feudal silhouette of his house against the sky. In the bedroom, his servant opened the wardrobes and brought out the famous shirts, and then Gatsby did something Nick never forgot: he played for Daisy on the piano, or rather had his boarder Klipspringer play, a popular song of the day about having fun though they had no money. The irony was lost on no one except perhaps Gatsby himself. Daisy, listening, seemed to understand for the first time the scale of the fiction Gatsby had constructed: a whole life built, brick by brick, out of the hope of this afternoon.

The following Saturday, Daisy came to one of Gatsby's parties, and the evening revealed the fault lines. She was appalled by the crowd, by the raw, loud, newly-rich energy of it all, so different from the polished East Egg gatherings she knew. Tom, who had come along, prowled the party like a detective, and afterward he told Daisy and Nick with heavy significance that he had investigated Gatsby and knew things. Daisy defended Gatsby weakly, but Nick could see she was shaken. The party that had been Gatsby's great instrument for winning Daisy had become, now that she was actually there, an embarrassment. It was the first sign that Gatsby's dream and Daisy's reality might not fit together after all.

In the weeks that followed, the affair settled into a dangerous routine. Daisy visited Gatsby's house; they lunched together; Gatsby grew more confident and more possessive. He told Nick he wanted Daisy to leave Tom, to say she had never loved him, to wipe the marriage out as if it had never happened. Nick tried to warn him that the past could not be repeated, that Daisy was not the girl of 1917 but a married woman with a child and a whole life built on money. Gatsby brushed the warning aside. He had waited five years; he was not going to be reasonable now. Nick watched his friend with growing dread, admiring his devotion and fearing its end in equal measure. The dream was at its brightest just before it burned out.
chapters.title: The Reunion

paragraphs: The confrontation came on the hottest day of the summer. Tom, Daisy, Gatsby, Nick, and Jordan drove into Manhattan to escape the heat and ended up in a stifling suite at the Plaza Hotel, with whiskey and the city shimmering below. The air was thick with tension. Tom had begun to suspect the truth about Daisy and Gatsby, and Gatsby, emboldened by weeks of secret happiness, decided the moment had come to claim Daisy openly. What followed was one of the great scenes in American fiction: two men fighting over a woman who sat between them, wilting in the heat, while the afternoon burned away outside.

Tom struck first, with the blunt weapon of class. He attacked Gatsby's past, his money, his parties, demanding to know where he had really gone to school and how he had really made his fortune. He had done some investigating and flung the word at Gatsby like a stone: bootlegger. Gatsby answered with dignity at first, then with growing fury, and finally he said the thing he had come to say: Daisy loved him, and had always loved him, and Tom was finished. He turned to Daisy and demanded that she tell Tom, there and then, that she had never loved him. Just say it, he urged her. Say you never loved him.

Daisy tried. She looked at Tom and said she loved Gatsby, but when Gatsby pressed her to deny that she had ever loved Tom at all, she broke. She cried out that he was asking too much of her, that she could not lie about the past, that she had loved Tom once, whatever else was true now. Tom seized the moment like the brute he was, pressing his advantage, reminding Daisy of their daughter, of their marriage, of everything real and solid that Gatsby's dream could not touch. And Daisy, confronted at last with a choice between the dream and the life, chose the life. She chose Tom, not out of love but out of the instinct of her class: Tom was safe, Tom was rich in the old established way, Tom would always be there. Gatsby's face fell. Nick saw the defeat in it, the terrible realization that the dream was dead, that Daisy was not the girl of Louisville but a careless, frightened woman who would never leave her world for his.

The party broke up in ruins. Tom, magnanimous in victory, insisted that Daisy drive home with Gatsby in Gatsby's yellow car, a final humiliation disguised as generosity. They left together, Daisy and Gatsby, in the yellow roadster, with Tom following behind with Nick and Jordan. The dream had lasted one afternoon at the Plaza. By evening it was over, though Gatsby did not know it yet. He still believed, driving home through the gathering dark with Daisy beside him, that everything would be all right, that she would leave Tom and they would begin again. He believed it because he had to. The alternative was unthinkable.

The day began with a desperate suggestion. Trapped in the Buchanan house by the brutal heat, Daisy proposed they all go into the city, and Tom, eager to show his dominance, agreed at once. They drove in: Tom taking Gatsby's yellow car with Jordan and Nick, Gatsby driving Tom's blue coupé with Daisy, a pointed exchange of vehicles that Tom intended as a joke and Gatsby endured as a humiliation. In the city they took a suite at the Plaza, ordered whiskey and mint juleps, and tried to be gay. But the heat pressed down, the whiskey loosened tongues, and the afternoon curdled. Daisy, restless and reckless, let her hand rest near Gatsby's, and Tom saw it. The pretense was over.

Tom had come prepared. He had hired a detective, or so he claimed, and he laid out what he knew: Gatsby's drugstores, the bootlegging, the connection to Wolfsheim. He said the word aloud, slowly, savoring it. Gatsby, who had faced the afternoon with the poise of a man sure of his cause, began to come apart. His polished old sport cracked; he called Tom an idiot and a fool; he lost the beautiful manners that had been his armor. Daisy watched the two men and saw, with terrible clarity, what Nick had seen all along: Gatsby was not of her world. He was a pretender, however gorgeous his pretense, and Tom, for all his brutality, was the real thing, solid and unassailable in his money.

The cruelest moment came when Gatsby, desperate, demanded that Daisy do the impossible. He wanted her to tell Tom she had never loved him, to erase five years of marriage with a sentence. Daisy tried to obey, but the words would not come out as Gatsby needed them. She loved Gatsby, she said, but she had loved Tom too, once, and she could not lie about it. It was the truth, and it destroyed Gatsby. Nick saw his friend's face change as he understood: the dream he had carried for five years had just died in a hotel room, killed not by Tom's money but by Daisy's honesty. Daisy was not the green light. She was a woman, flawed and frightened, and she would never be what Gatsby needed her to be.

Tom's victory was total and ugly. He lectured Gatsby on the sanctity of marriage with staggering hypocrisy, this man who kept a mistress in the valley of ashes, and Daisy let him. She let him because Tom offered what Gatsby could not: safety, solidity, the unthinking confidence of old money. When they finally left the Plaza, Tom's parting cruelty was to send Daisy home in Gatsby's yellow car with Gatsby driving, as if to prove that he feared nothing. Nick rode back with Tom and Jordan, sick at heart, watching the yellow car disappear ahead into the dusk. He did not know that within the hour, everything would be worse than he could imagine.
chapters.title: The Plaza Hotel

paragraphs: On the way home from the Plaza, driving Gatsby's big yellow car through the gathering dusk, Daisy struck and killed Myrtle Wilson. It happened in the valley of ashes, in front of Wilson's garage. Myrtle had quarreled with her husband that afternoon, and Tom, stopping for gas on the way into New York, had said something that made Wilson lock Myrtle upstairs. She had broken out, desperate and half-mad, and run into the road just as the yellow car came over the rise. The car did not slow. It swerved slightly, then raced on into the darkness, leaving Myrtle's body broken in the dust. Witnesses remembered the yellow car. Everyone in the valley of ashes knew whose car was yellow.

George Wilson, the pale, hollow-eyed garage owner, was destroyed. He had already suspected his wife of infidelity; he had found an expensive dog collar in her drawer and begun to understand. Now she was dead, and his grief turned slowly into a murderous purpose. He would not eat, he would not sleep; he rocked and muttered in the garage while his neighbor Michaelis sat with him through the night. Wilson became convinced that the driver of the yellow car had also been Myrtle's lover, the man who had ruined her, and he vowed to find him. He talked of God, of an all-seeing eye. Above the valley stood a huge faded billboard, the eyes of an oculist named T. J. Eckleburg, staring out over the ashes, and Wilson began to speak to those eyes as if they were the eyes of God himself, demanding justice.

Tom Buchanan, stopping at the garage that evening on his way home, made everything worse. Wilson told him the yellow car had killed Myrtle, and Tom, weeping crookedly with what may have been grief or only self-pity, let Wilson believe that the car belonged to Gatsby and that Gatsby had been Myrtle's lover. It was a lie that would kill a man: the car was Gatsby's, yes, but Daisy had been driving it, and it was Tom himself who had been Myrtle's lover all along. Tom fed Wilson the story that would send him after Gatsby, and then he drove home to Daisy, and together they sat down to their own dinner as if nothing had happened. Nick would remember it as the defining truth about Tom and Daisy: they were careless people, they smashed up things and creatures and then retreated back into their money, and let other people clean up the mess.

The disaster had been building all afternoon in the valley of ashes. Wilson, hollow-eyed and sick, had finally confronted his wife. He had found the jeweled dog collar hidden in her drawer, proof of a lover with money, and his slow mind had pieced together enough of the truth. He told Myrtle they were leaving, going west, getting away from whatever was poisoning her, and when she raged and fought him, he locked her in the upstairs room. Myrtle Wilson was not a woman who could be locked in a room. She had spent eleven years married to a man she despised, dreaming of the rich life she glimpsed through Tom Buchanan, and she would rather die than go back to being nothing. She forced the window, climbed down, and ran.

Michaelis, who kept the coffee house next door, saw it happen and would tell the story later to the police. Myrtle came running out of the garage into the road, waving her arms, as if she recognized the big yellow car or thought she recognized the man driving it. The car was coming fast over the rise, much too fast for the dusty road. It did not slow down. It struck her and kept going, and by the time Michaelis reached her, she was dead, her life spilled out on the road she had dreamed of escaping. Within the hour, the whole valley knew: the death car was yellow, and everyone knew whose car was yellow.

Tom's stop at the garage that evening sealed Gatsby's fate. He came with Nick and Jordan, on the drive home from New York, and pushed through the crowd to where Wilson sat rocking with grief. Wilson told him about the yellow car, about the lover, about his vow of revenge. And Tom, with tears in his eyes that may have been for Myrtle or only for himself, told Wilson that the car belonged to Jay Gatsby. He said it as if it were the whole truth. He never mentioned that Daisy had been at the wheel. He never mentioned that the lover Wilson was hunting was Tom himself. Nick stood a few feet away and heard every word, and he said nothing, and the silence would haunt him. Tom had just aimed a loaded gun at an innocent man, and Nick had watched him pull the trigger with words.

That night, in the Buchanan house in East Egg, dinner was served as usual. Nick went there almost against his will, drawn by a dreadful curiosity, and found Tom and Daisy composed at their table, talking of ordinary things. They were planning to leave town for a while, to get away until the unpleasantness blew over. Daisy was pale but calm; Tom was expansive, almost cheerful. Myrtle Wilson lay dead in Queens. George Wilson was loading his pistol. And the Buchanans ate their dinner and discussed their travel plans, insulated by money from every consequence of the wreckage they had made. Nick sat among them in silence, understanding at last the full meaning of carelessness. He left the house that night and walked over to Gatsby's, where his friend stood alone in the dark, waiting for a telephone call that would never come.
chapters.title: The Yellow Car

paragraphs: That night, Gatsby kept his vigil. He stood outside the Buchanan house in the dark, watching Daisy's windows, waiting in case Tom tried to hurt her, waiting for the telephone call that would tell him she was leaving Tom and coming to him. Nick found him there in the small hours and tried to make him see the truth: Daisy had chosen, the dream was over, he should go away before it got worse. Gatsby would not hear it. He insisted on waiting. He told Nick what had really happened on the road: Daisy had been driving, Daisy had killed Myrtle, and he had taken the blame without a second thought. He would take any blame for Daisy. He waited all night in the darkness, and no call came. In the morning, Nick left him sitting on the steps of his empty mansion, and went to work in the city.

When Nick returned that afternoon, Gatsby was still alive, and they had their last conversation. Gatsby was oddly calm now, almost cheerful, talking about the past as if it were still the future: about Daisy, about how they would go away together, about how it would all work out. Nick, looking at him, felt a sudden wave of pity and admiration for this man who had poured his whole soul into a dream. Before leaving, Nick said something he had never said to anyone, and would never say again: he told Gatsby that he was worth the whole rotten crowd put together. It was the only compliment Nick ever paid him, and the truest thing in the book. Then Nick went into the house, and Gatsby went down to his pool.

He had not used the pool all summer. Now, on that cool autumn afternoon, he had the mattress inflated and carried it down to the water, as if he meant to finally enjoy the things he had bought. He lay on the mattress in his bathing suit, drifting, looking up at the sky. George Wilson came through the trees with a pistol. Wilson had learned from Tom that the yellow car belonged to Gatsby, and in his maddened grief he had decided that Gatsby was the man who had stolen his wife and then run her down. He shot Gatsby in the pool and then turned the gun on himself. The gardener found them both later: Gatsby floating on the mattress, the gun still in Wilson's hand nearby. The dreamer and the cuckold, dead together on the most beautiful afternoon of the fall. Nick would learn the details later, from Michaelis and the police. What mattered was this: Gatsby died still believing in Daisy, still waiting for her call, and Daisy never called.

Gatsby's vigil lasted all night. He stood in the dark outside the Buchanan house, among the shadows of the lawn, watching the windows. One by one the lights went out, until only the hall light remained, and then that too went dark. He waited in case Tom tried to harm Daisy in his rage, waited in case she needed him, waited above all for the telephone to ring with her voice telling him she was leaving Tom. Nick, who found him there in the small hours, tried everything: reason, pleading, the plain facts of the afternoon at the Plaza. Gatsby would not move. He had waited five years for Daisy; he could wait one night. The stars wheeled overhead, the bay lapped at the shore, and Gatsby stood his ground in the dark, the last faithful lover in a faithless world.

It was during that long night that Gatsby told Nick the truth about the accident. Daisy had been driving, he said quietly, as if it were the most natural thing in the world. She had been driving, she had lost her nerve, and he had taken charge afterward: he had told her to stop, he had driven the rest of the way, he would take whatever blame there was. There was no hesitation in him, no calculation. If Daisy had killed someone, then Gatsby would be the killer. That was what love meant to him: total, unquestioning absorption of the beloved's guilt. Nick listened and understood that Gatsby would have done the same for any crime, any disaster. His devotion was absolute, and absolutely doomed.

Morning came gray and cool, the first real autumn day. Gatsby was still at the house when Nick left for the city, sitting on the steps of his empty mansion in the dawn light, and he was still there, in spirit, when Nick returned that afternoon. He had the strange calm of a man who has decided everything will be fine. He talked about the past as if it were the future: about Daisy, about how they would go away together, about the life they would have. Nick looked at him and felt his throat close. He wanted to warn him, to tell him about Wilson, about Tom's lie, about the gun. But Gatsby was beyond warning. He had the mattress inflated for the pool, a thing he had never once used all summer, as if he meant to finally enjoy his own possessions. He went down to the water in his bathing suit, and Nick went into the house, and that was the last time Nick ever saw him alive.

Wilson came through the trees with the pistol in his coat. He had walked all the way from the valley of ashes, past the billboard eyes of T. J. Eckleburg, driven by grief and by Tom Buchanan's lie. He found Gatsby floating on the mattress in the pool, looking up at the sky, and he fired. Then he turned the gun on himself. The gardener found them both in the late afternoon: Gatsby on the mattress, blood spreading in the clear water, and Wilson a little way off in the grass with the pistol beside him. The chauffeur heard the shots, and the butler, and the servants came running, but it was too late for both men. Gatsby died as he had lived that summer: alone among his beautiful things, believing in Daisy to the very end. The green light was still burning across the bay. Daisy never called.
chapters.title: The Vigil and the Shot

paragraphs: Nick took charge of the funeral, because there was no one else to do it. He telephoned and telegraphed everyone Gatsby had ever known: the hundreds of guests who had drunk his champagne and danced on his lawns all summer, the business associates, the friends. Nobody came. Meyer Wolfsheim, the gangster who had made Gatsby, sent a letter saying he could not get mixed up in it, that he had his own life to think of. Klipspringer, the boarder who had lived off Gatsby for months, telephoned only to ask whether Nick could forward a pair of tennis shoes he had left behind. Daisy sent nothing at all, not even a flower. She and Tom had left town the day after the murder, gone traveling, as careless people do, leaving others to bury the dead.

On the day of the funeral it rained. The only mourners were Nick, Gatsby's father, a few servants, the postman, and one unexpected guest: the owl-eyed man from Gatsby's library, the guest who had once marveled that Gatsby's books were real, with real pages and everything. He had come a long way, he said, to pay his respects. He took off his glasses and wiped them, and remarked that poor Gatsby deserved better than this empty room. Gatsby's father, Henry C. Gatz of Minnesota, arrived with his son's childhood schedule of self-improvement, the plan written in the back of the cowboy novel, and showed it to Nick with trembling pride. He said his boy would have been a great man if he had lived. Nick, standing in the rain at the graveside, understood the terrible arithmetic of Gatsby's life: he had given everything to people who gave nothing back, and in the end the only ones who came were a stranger, an old man, and the friend who had known him least and loved him best.

After the funeral, Nick's disillusionment was complete. He tried to see Jordan one last time, but their affair, which had never been more than a pleasant distraction, dissolved in mutual coldness; she told him she had always thought him honest, and now she was not so sure. He ran into Tom on Fifth Avenue in October, and Tom, with staggering shamelessness, claimed he had told Wilson the truth about the car because he had owed it to Myrtle, and then announced that he had cried like a baby when he heard Gatsby was dead. Nick refused to shake his hand. He understood at last what Tom and Daisy were: careless people who smashed up things and creatures and retreated back into their money or their vast carelessness, letting other people clean up the mess they had made. Nick wanted no more of the East. He packed up, settled Gatsby's affairs, and went home to the Middle West, to the clean, honest dullness of the place he had come from.

The days after the murder were a study in ingratitude. Nick telephoned everyone he could think of, everyone who had ever drunk Gatsby's champagne or danced on his lawns, and the responses were a litany of excuses. The phone at the mansion was disconnected, or answered by servants who knew nothing. Meyer Wolfsheim, the man who had raised Gatsby up in the world, replied with a letter full of elaborate regret: he had been like a son to Gatsby, he said, but he could not get mixed up in this, he had his own life and his own business to protect. It was the underworld's version of a condolence card, and Nick read it with disgust. The great man's friends were evaporating like mist.

The worst call came from Klipspringer, the boarder who had lived off Gatsby for months, playing the piano and eating his food. Klipspringer telephoned Nick long distance, and for a moment Nick thought he was coming to the funeral. Instead he wanted to know whether Nick could send on a pair of tennis shoes he had left at the house. That was the sum of his grief: a pair of shoes. Daisy sent nothing at all. No flowers, no note, no word. She and Tom had vanished, gone traveling as careless people do when the mess gets too deep. Nick thought of all the afternoons Daisy had spent in that house, all the promises in her golden voice, and felt something cold settle in his chest.

Then, out of the gray Minnesota distance, came Henry C. Gatz. Gatsby's father arrived by train, an old man in a cheap suit, bewildered and proud, and Nick took him to the mansion his son had built. The old man wandered through the empty rooms, touching the furniture, and showed Nick his most precious possession: a ragged copy of a cowboy novel, with a schedule written on the flyleaf in a boy's hand, the plan for self-improvement that James Gatz had drawn up at seventeen. The old man read it aloud with tears in his eyes, certain that his boy would have been a great man. Nick looked at the old man's pride and the empty mansion and the rain beginning to fall, and thought that this, this worn book and this grieving father, was the truest thing left of Jay Gatsby.

The funeral was held in the rain. The minister came, the postman came, a few servants came, and the owl-eyed man from the library, who had driven a long way to pay his respects to the man whose books were real. That was all. No Daisy, no Tom, no Jordan, none of the hundreds who had crowded the parties. Nick stood at the graveside in the wet grass and watched the coffin go down, thinking of Gatsby's smile, his hope, his arms stretched out toward the green light. Afterward, Nick broke with Jordan, whose cool dishonesty he could no longer bear, and in October he met Tom by chance on Fifth Avenue. Tom spoke of Myrtle with crude sentiment and claimed he had done the right thing telling Wilson about the car. Nick refused to shake his hand. He settled Gatsby's affairs, closed up the mansion, and bought his ticket west. He had come east to make his fortune. He was going home with nothing but the story, and the story was enough.
chapters.title: The Empty Funeral

paragraphs: Before leaving the East for good, Nick went down to the beach one last time and sat on the sand where Gatsby's mansion threw its shadow over the water. He thought about everything he had seen that summer: the parties, the shirts, the Plaza, the yellow car, the pool. And he thought about Gatsby, and about the green light at the end of Daisy's dock, and slowly his mind widened beyond Gatsby to something larger. He imagined the first Dutch sailors who had come up this shore four hundred years before, seeing the fresh green breast of the new world, and feeling the same wonder Gatsby must have felt when he first picked out the green light. For a transitory enchanted moment, man must have held his breath before this continent, compelled into an aesthetic contemplation he neither understood nor desired, face to face for the last time in history with something commensurate to his capacity for wonder.

Gatsby's wonder had been Daisy, or what Daisy stood for: the green light, the promise that life could be remade, that the past could be recovered, that wealth and love and beauty could all be his if he only wanted them hard enough. Nick understood now that Gatsby had been right to believe and wrong about everything else. The dream itself was beautiful; it was the world that was corrupt. Gatsby had paid a high price for living too long with a single dream, and in the end the dream had outlasted the dreamer, as dreams do.

And so Nick's meditation becomes everyone's. The green light is not just Daisy's dock; it is the future itself, the orgastic future that recedes before us year by year, always just out of reach. We chase it, we believe in it, we stretch out our arms toward it, and it eludes us, and still we run faster tomorrow. That is the human condition as Fitzgerald saw it: we are all Gatsby, reaching across dark water toward a light we can never touch, and the reaching is both our glory and our doom.
So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.

On his last night in West Egg, Nick walked over to Gatsby's empty house and found that some boy had written an obscene word on the white steps in chalk. He scrubbed it out with his shoe, erasing it completely, as if to protect Gatsby's memory from even that small defilement. The mansion stood dark and silent behind him, the pool covered, the gardens overgrown. All the music and laughter of the summer seemed like a dream someone else had dreamed. Nick stood there for a long time, thinking about the man who had believed so completely in the green light, and about how little the world had deserved his belief.

That is why the novel's ending belongs to everyone. We all have our green lights: the future we imagine, the person we want to become, the happiness we are certain lies just across the water. Fitzgerald's genius was to see that this longing is both the most beautiful and the most dangerous thing about us. It makes us reach, and strive, and sometimes build mansions out of nothing. And it makes us blind, because the light always recedes, year by year, no matter how fast we run. Gatsby's tragedy was to mistake the light for a destination. Our wisdom, if we have any, is to keep reaching anyway, knowing the current will always bear us back.
chapters.title: So We Beat On
